November 19, 2064.
When we pulled back near Klintsy, heavy snow began to fall.
I opened the last can of beef. The cold chunks of meat were covered with a layer of white fat.
This was Roma's legacy. I shoved a mouthful down. It felt like swallowing a stone, sinking heavily into my gut.
We shared the can among us. It was a bit salty. There was still some water in the truck, but everyone drank sparingly, and we passed one bottle back to the men in the vehicle behind.
One of the wounded came down with a fever. We gave him a shot of antibiotics and prayed he'd hold out.
I checked the medkit and what water we had left, told Dentist we'd need to figure out resupply soon.
Dentist just smiled and said once we reached the Yellow Zone, getting supplies wouldn't be a problem for us.
I asked him if that meant we'd be reduced to bandits from here on out.
Dentist's face went dark. He kept driving. Snow flurried in the headlights. Nobody said another word.
After Klintsy, command reached Dentist. They said the main force was retreating towards the border, but Moscow's troops were pressing close. They asked if we could cover the withdrawal.
There was guilt in that voice over the comms. Dentist didn't answer right away. He asked where the General was. Command fell silent, then said the General was dead.
My head went blank. There was ringing in my skull. I couldn't think straight.
Dentist pressed for details. They said when the command center was overrun, the General saved the last bullet for himself.
I couldn't believe it. Didn't want to. How could the General go out so feebly? Why didn't they tell us yesterday?

The comms kept spitting words—"defeat", "Relics"—but I was too furious, started cursing non-stop. Someone in back bawled out loud and I screamed at him to shut up... though my own face was wet with tears.
Even now, writing this entry, I still can't come to terms with it.
The General was like a pine tree to us, like a banner standing tall.
I'll never forget the first time I saw him, on the podium, telling us what country meant, what civilization meant, what the KCCO fought for.
Now the sun has come up. Dentist moved the wounded into the truck behind, told them to link up with the main force at the border.
I handed over the last two doses of antibiotics. The brother with the fever was burning hot, unconscious. I just hope he makes it in time.
Then we waved them off, and drove in the opposite direction.
This is our motherland. This is our land.
